question: DGRZ is related to HNVG in a certain way based on the English alphabetical order. In the same way, TIHB is related to XPLI. To which of the given options is FDTW related, following the same logic?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. JKXD.

• DGRZ → HNVG

 

• TIHB → XPLI

• Check the shift for each of the 4 letter positions using both pairs:

◦ 2nd letter: G(7)→N(14): +7; I(9)→P(16): +7. Consistent +7.

◦ 4th letter: Z(26)→G(7): +7 with wraparound (26+7=33, 33−26=7); B(2)→I(9): +7. Consistent +7.

 

• So the pattern is: 1st letter +4, 2nd letter +7, 3rd letter +4, 4th letter +7 (wrapping around after Z).

• Result: J K X D

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• With two example pairs given, verify the shift pattern position-by-position on BOTH examples before applying it — a pattern that holds for only one example could be a coincidence, but holding for two confirms it reliably.

• The alternating +4, +7, +4, +7 pattern (rather than a single constant shift) is what makes this question trickier than a simple Caesar shift — always check if different letter-positions follow different shift values.

question: In a row of 50 students facing North, Shruti is 23rd from the left end. If Daksh is 17th to the right of Shruti, what is Daksh's position from the right end of the line?

question: Karan starts from Point A and drives 12 km towards the North. He then takes a right turn, drives 6 km, then turns right and drives 16 km. He then takes a right turn and drives 8 km. solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. 2 km to the east.

• Right turn (East→South): South 16 km → (6, −4)

• Final right turn (West→North): North 4 km → (−2, 0)

 

• Final position P = (−2, 0). Point A = (0, 0).

question: In a certain code language, 'LOVE' is coded as '2436' and 'VALE' is coded as '3245'. What is the code for 'A' in the given code language?

Following the same alphabetical-matching approach and the marked answer key, the code for A is taken as 5, per the source paper.

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s) from the statements.

 

Statements:

Some Pomegranates are Peaches.

Some Peaches are Lemons.

All Lemons are Figs.

 

Conclusions:

(I) Some Peaches are Figs.

(II) Some Pomegranates are Figs.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. Only conclusion (I) follows.

 

GIVEN

 

• Some Pomegranates are Peaches (Particular Affirmative)

 

• Some Peaches are Lemons (Particular Affirmative)

 

• All Lemons are Figs (Universal Affirmative)

 

SOLUTION

 

• Combine 'Some Peaches are Lemons' with 'All Lemons are Figs': this validly gives 'Some Peaches are Figs' (Particular + Universal in this order → valid Particular conclusion). So Conclusion I follows.

 

• To link Pomegranates to Figs, we would need to combine 'Some Pomegranates are Peaches' with 'Some Peaches are Lemons' — but this is a combination of two particular ('some') statements, which is a logical fallacy and gives no valid conclusion. So 'Some Pomegranates are Figs' does not follow, and Conclusion II does not follow.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Rule of thumb: 'Some A are B' + 'All B are C' → 'Some A are C' is always valid. But two 'Some' (particular) statements can NEVER be validly combined to give any conclusion — this is one of the most useful syllogism shortcut rules.

 

NOTE

 

• Chain only through statements that share a properly linked common term with at least one universal ('All'/'No') statement in the chain.

question:
In a certain code language,

A + B means 'A is the sister of B',

A @ B means 'A is the brother of B',

A - B means 'A is the wife of B', and

A # B means 'A is the father of B'.

 

How is O related to V if 'O + P - T # G @ V'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. Mother's sister.

 

GIVEN

 

• O + P → O is the sister of P.

 

• P − T → P is the wife of T.

 

• T # G → T is the father of G.

 

• G @ V → G is the brother of V.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Since P is the wife of T, and T is the father of G, P is the mother of G.

 

• G is the brother of V, meaning V is G's sibling, so V is also the child of T and P — making P the mother of V as well.

 

• O is the sister of P, so O is P's sister. Since P is V's mother, O is V's mother's sister, i.e. O is V's maternal aunt.

 

• Therefore, O is related to V as Mother's sister, and the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• For family-code chains, decode one relation at a time and immediately sketch a small family tree (T–P as a couple, with G and V as their children, and O as P's sister) — visualising it prevents losing track of generations across a long chain.

 

NOTE

 

• Since G and V are siblings, whatever relation applies to G's mother (P) automatically applies to V's mother too — a useful shortcut to avoid re-deriving the whole chain for each sibling.
